reference.title: Twisting Crunch
reference.listing: Video; data sheet: body part Waist, equipment Body weight, exercise type Strength

breathing.pattern: Exhale as you curl and turn, inhale as you lower.
breathing.cadence: About 1 s up and turn, a short squeeze, about 1.4 s down, then switch sides

prescription.tempo: About 1 s up, brief pause, 1.5 s down, alternating
prescription.progression: Slower lowering and a 2 s hold, then bicycle crunch

cues.text: Lie on your back, knees bent about 90 degrees, feet flat. Fingertips lightly behind the head, elbows wide.
Breathe out, curl up and turn the right shoulder toward the left knee; lead with the shoulder, not the elbow.
Short squeeze. Both elbows stay open; the low back and hips stay on the mat.
Breathe in and lower slowly back to the centre.
Repeat to the other side: left shoulder toward the right knee.
Lower under control and rest the head briefly.

mistakes.mistake: Pulling the elbow across with the arm
mistakes.fix: Keep both elbows wide; turn the rib cage, not the arm.
Fingertips only; look up past the knees.

mistakes.mistake: Hips rocking or the feet lifting
mistakes.fix: Keep the pelvis heavy and the feet flat.

mistakes.mistake: Turning without curling (lying flat and rolling)
mistakes.fix: Lift the shoulder blades first, then turn.

kinematics.measure: Upper trunk (T12 to C7) from the floor
kinematics.norm: Shoulder blades clear the mat as in a crunch (clinical opinion)
Upper trunk turns toward the opposite knee; the cross curl-up raised external oblique activity (Konrad 2001)
Most of the curl happens here (clinical opinion)
Knees about 90 degrees, feet flat; the pelvis does not move (clinical opinion)
Hands support the head only; elbows stay wide (clinical opinion)
Controlled, about 1 s up and 1.5 s down (clinical opinion)

sources.title: Konrad, Schmitz and Denner 2001, neuromuscular evaluation of trunk-training exercises (J Athl Train 36(2):109-118; PMC155519)
Crommert, Bjerkefors, Tarassova and Ekblom 2021, abdominal muscle activation during common modifications of the trunk curl-up exercise (J Strength Cond Res 35(2):428-435; PMID 29319600)
Escamilla, Lewis, Pecson, Imamura and Andrews 2016, muscle activation among supine, prone and side position exercises with and without a Swiss ball (Sports Health 8(4):372-379; PMC4922527)
McGill 1998, low back exercises: evidence for improving exercise regimens (Phys Ther 78(7):754-765; PMID 9672547)

cautions: Stop if you feel sharp, radiating or nerve-type pain.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.

Low-back pain, disc problems or flexion intolerance: start with a McGill-style curl-up, dead bug or plank; partial curl-ups gave the best abdominal challenge for the least spine compression in one model study (Axler and McGill 1997).
Combined flexion and twisting under fatigue is a common trigger of back pain; keep the reps controlled and stop the set when form slips (clinical opinion).
Pregnancy and postpartum (diastasis recti): get individual guidance before dynamic trunk-flexion work.
Osteoporosis or vertebral fracture: avoid repeated loaded spinal flexion and twisting.
The athlete mesh rests on the mat; the rig collision shapes are thicker than the mesh at the back and buttocks, so floorTolerance records how far those proxy shapes sink below the mat surface.
modify: Neck pain: cross the arms on the chest and turn the chest.
regressions: Arms reaching across to the outside of the knee (no hands behind the head).
progressions: Slow 3 s lowering with a 2 s hold.

muscleNotes.obliques_r: External oblique on the side of the turning shoulder and internal oblique on the other side rotate the curling trunk: external oblique rose to about 36% MVC in a cross (twisting) curl-up versus 29% in a straight curl-up (Konrad 2001); internal oblique and transversus were more active turning one way and external oblique the other (Crommert 2021).
muscleNotes.obliques_l: External oblique on the side of the turning shoulder and internal oblique on the other side rotate the curling trunk: external oblique rose to about 36% MVC in a cross (twisting) curl-up versus 29% in a straight curl-up (Konrad 2001); internal oblique and transversus were more active turning one way and external oblique the other (Crommert 2021).
muscleNotes.core: Rectus abdominis still curls the trunk: about 56% MVC in the cross curl-up (Konrad 2001), and it did not change with the twist direction (Crommert 2021).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_r: Stay quiet and only steady the bent legs (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.hip_flexors_l: Stay quiet and only steady the bent legs (clinical opinion).
